title: Stop trusting the database: signing your options table
excerpt: A compromised admin account can rewrite wp_options without touching a single file. Here is how to detect it — and why file-integrity scanners never will.

title: Why I moved my build pipeline off GitHub Actions — and what it cost
excerpt: Forty minutes of CI a day is two working weeks a year. The math finally caught up with me.

title: PHP 8.5 readonly classes are the feature nobody asked for and everybody needed
excerpt: A small language feature that quietly ends a whole category of bug report.

title: The block editor is a document model. Treat it like one.
excerpt: Every editor bug I have fixed this year came from someone forgetting that block markup is data, not HTML.

title: Composer lockfiles are a security control
excerpt: Pinning a version is not paranoia. It is the only part of the supply chain you actually control.

title: On writing a WordPress theme in 2026
excerpt: The block theme finally feels like the platform the block editor always promised.

title: Transients, object caches and the lie of “fast enough”
excerpt: Every cache layer is a promise you will eventually have to keep by hand.

title: Charge for the outcome, bill for the hour
excerpt: A consulting pricing model that survives contact with procurement.

title: The one-page operating agreement
excerpt: Everything a small consultancy actually needs in writing fits on one page, if you are honest about it.

title: Fire the client who pays late twice
excerpt: The first late payment is an accident. The second one is a policy.

title: Retainers are a promise about attention
excerpt: You are not selling hours. You are selling the fact that you already know the system.

title: What a CTO actually does all day
excerpt: Fewer decisions than you would think, and far more translation between rooms that do not talk to each other.

title: Your password manager's weakest link is the browser extension
excerpt: Threat-modeling the thing we all installed without thinking.

title: Nonces are not CSRF tokens
excerpt: They rhyme with CSRF tokens closely enough to get a lot of WordPress code quietly wrong.

title: Reading a CVE like an engineer
excerpt: Severity scores are for procurement. Here is what to read instead.

title: Disclosure timelines, from the other side of the inbox
excerpt: Ninety days is a courtesy, not a contract.

title: On praying for the people who file the bug reports
excerpt: Patience as an engineering discipline.

title: Sabbath for people who ship on Fridays
excerpt: Rest does not care whether the deploy went out clean.

The city council meeting nobody attends
excerpt: The meeting where the actual budget gets decided has three people in the room, and none of them are reporters.

title: Local news is infrastructure
excerpt: Nobody notices infrastructure until the week it stops working.

title: A rainbow over the rail yard
excerpt: Walking back from the coffee place there was a full rainbow over the rail yard, the kind that touches down at both ends. Two guys in hard hats stopped and took pictures, and for a second nobody said a word. So did I.

title: Two working weeks a year
excerpt: Forty minutes of CI a day, every day, adds up to two working weeks a year if you do the math. I did the math out loud at dinner and nobody at the table was impressed, but I was, and now I have to do something about it.

title: Rain, Psalm 46, a quiet build server
excerpt: The kind of morning where nothing is broken and you almost distrust the quiet, waiting for the other shoe. Read the psalm twice, once for the words and once for the part of me that still does not believe it. Left the server alone.

title: The CVE that was mostly marketing
excerpt: Read a vulnerability write-up today that spent more words on the logo than on the patch, which tells you who it was written for. Wrote a grumpy draft, then deleted the whole thing before publishing. This is growth, apparently, or so I am choosing to call it.

title: Marta finds the second ledger
excerpt: Chapter twelve is finally done, which means the reader learns what the first set of books was actually for. The second ledger only works if you believe the first one was the honest lie, and I had to decide, finally, which one I believed myself.

title: The bug that only reproduced on one machine
excerpt: Spent the morning fixing a bug that only reproduced on a coworker's machine, which is its own kind of humbling. Turned out to be a timezone assumption baked into a query I wrote two years ago and never once questioned since. Fixed it, wrote a test, moved on.

title: The long way home
excerpt: Took the long way home past the church tonight, mostly because the short way meant walking past the office again. The lights were still on up there, which used to bother me more than it does now. Some things get easier the longer you practice not answering.

title: A reader wrote back
excerpt: A reader emailed to say the newsletter arrived exactly when she needed it, which is the kind of message that makes the habit worth keeping on the weeks it feels pointless. I do not know what to do with compliments, so I wrote back and said thank you.

title: On finishing a draft you no longer believe in
excerpt: Sometimes the honest move is to finish the book you started, not the book you would write today.

title: Outlining for people who hate outlines
excerpt: A short outline you will actually follow beats a long one you will abandon by chapter three.

title: A Post From The Classic Editor
content:
This post was written in the classic editor, long before block markup existed.

It references a footnote1 from that era.

title: Hardening WordPress, part 1: the config file nobody re-reads
excerpt: Most `wp-config.php` files are written once, at launch, and never audited again.
